chapter_note.about: Verbal aptitude is 3 to 4 marks of the 15 aptitude marks, and most questions are quick. You will meet grammar fill-ins, vocabulary and analogies, reading inference, and sentence ordering. Each has a short method: name the relation, find the time marker, check the sound, or compare the option with the passage. Few marks need more than a minute.

concept_map.title: Tenses and verb forms
concept_map.one_line: Put the events on a time line, then pick the form for each one.

concept_map.title: Articles and prepositions
concept_map.one_line: Choose a or an by sound, and learn the fixed word pairs.

concept_map.title: Agreement and homophones
concept_map.one_line: Match the verb to the real subject, and check the meaning of sound-alike words.

concept_map.title: Vocabulary
concept_map.one_line: Guess the meaning from the sentence first, then match the option.

concept_map.title: Analogies
concept_map.one_line: Name the relation between the first pair, then apply the same relation in the same direction.

concept_map.title: Idioms and phrasal verbs
concept_map.one_line: Read the whole sentence, guess the meaning, and pick the chunk that matches.

concept_map.title: Reading inference
concept_map.one_line: Accept only what the passage supports, and strike extreme, future and outside-fact options.

concept_map.title: Sentence order and reference
concept_map.one_line: Find the opener with no back-reference, then follow pronouns and connectors.

concept_map.title: Conditionals and ambiguity
concept_map.one_line: A counterfactual describes what did not happen, and a pronoun must point to exactly one noun.

gate_patterns: Grammar fill-ins on tense, articles and prepositions, one mark each and the most common pattern. 10 questions from 2017 to 2026.
Vocabulary and analogies, including degree analogies since 2024. About 16 questions.
Reading inference and summary, 2 marks each, where extreme words and outside facts are the traps. 12 questions, plus a few sentence-ordering and idiom questions.
chapter_note.simple: Verbal aptitude is about using English correctly and reading carefully. For grammar, you match the verb to the time and the subject. For word questions, you use the rest of the sentence to guess the meaning, and name how two words are related before looking at the choices. For reading questions, you accept only what the passage says, and ignore words like 'always' or 'never'. For jumbled sentences, you start with the one that makes sense alone and follow the pronouns.

cards.title: Tenses and verb forms
cards.simple: Tenses tell the listener when something happened. If two things happened in the past, you need a way to say which came first. Say the train left at 5:00 and you reached the station at 5:10. Your arrival is the main past event, so it takes the plain past form, 'reached'. The train's leaving came earlier, so it takes the 'had' form: 'had left'. In exam words: simple past for a finished event, past perfect (had + past participle) for the earlier of two past events, and present perfect (have/has + participle) for a past event linked to now.
cards.idea: 'The train ___ before we reached the station.' Two things happened in the past, and the train's leaving came first. English marks the earlier event with **had + past participle**: 'had left'. The later event stays in simple past: 'reached'. Put the events on a time line before you choose any verb form.
cards.idea_full:
'The train ___ before we reached the station.' Two things happened in the past, and the train's leaving came first. English marks the earlier event with **had + past participle**, the **past perfect**: 'had left'. The later event stays in simple past: 'reached'.

Simple past is for a finished event with a time marker (yesterday, in 2019). Present perfect (have/has + participle) links a past event to now, so it cannot go with a finished time such as yesterday. Continuous forms (was waiting) show an action in progress.
cards.definition:
Simple past: verb + -ed or an irregular form (went, saw).

Past perfect: had + past participle (had left). Use it for the earlier of two past events.

Present perfect: have/has + past participle (has gone). Use it for a past event with a result now, or one that began in the past and continues. Never use it with a finished time word.

Continuous: be + verb-ing (was waiting). Use it for an action in progress at that time.

Symbols: the past participle is the third form of the verb (go, went, gone).
cards.intuition_full: Draw a line with 'now' at the right end. Each event is a dot on it. When the story has two past dots, the left dot is the earlier one. The later dot is told in plain simple past, and the earlier dot gets 'had' to say 'this was already over by then'. The present perfect is different: it looks back from now, so it describes a past event as it matters today ('I have lost my keys' means I still do not have them). That is why it clashes with 'yesterday' or 'last year', which pin the event to a finished stretch of the past with no link to now. Most grammar fill-ins are solved by finding the time marker and asking which of these relationships it creates.

example.setup: Fill in: 'The train ___ (leave) before we reached the station.'
steps: Two past events: the train leaving and our reaching the station. Put them on a time line and ask which came first.
'We reached the station' is the later event, in simple past: reached.
The train left earlier than that. It is a past event that happened before another past event.
The earlier past takes the past perfect: had + past participle. The blank is 'had left'.

examples.setup: Fill in: 'The train ___ (leave) before we reached the station.'
steps: Two past events: the train leaving and our reaching the station. Put them on a time line and ask which came first.
'We reached the station' is the later event, in simple past: reached.
The train left earlier than that. It is a past event that happened before another past event.
The earlier past takes the past perfect: had + past participle. The blank is 'had left'.

examples.setup: Choose the correct sentence. (A) He has gone to Delhi yesterday. (B) He went to Delhi yesterday.
steps: Find the time marker: 'yesterday', a finished point in the past.
Present perfect (has gone) cannot go with a finished time marker.
Simple past is the form for a finished event at a stated time: went.
So sentence B is correct.

examples.setup: Which is acceptable: 'The rain stopped before we left' or 'The rain had stopped before we left'?
steps: Both events are named, and 'before' already tells the order.
Because the order is clear from the connector, simple past is enough.
Past perfect is also correct, and stresses that the rain was already over.
If only one of the two appears among the options, pick that one.
examples.answer: Both are correct. 'Before' and 'after' make the order clear, so past perfect is optional there.

cards.why: Tense questions are the most common 1-mark grammar items in GATE. A time line turns a guess into a check. In GATE: a sentence with a blank, four verb forms, and one time marker that decides the answer.
how: Find the time marker or the second event in the sentence.
Draw a quick time line and place the events.
Earlier of two past events: had + participle. Finished time: simple past. Link to now: present perfect.
Check the subject agrees with the verb, then re-read.
cards.mistake: Using present perfect with a finished time such as yesterday or last year, for example 'He has gone yesterday'. The time word shuts the event off from now. Use simple past there.
edge_cases: 'Since' and 'for' go with present perfect when the action continues to now.
Past perfect needs two past events. A lone past event uses simple past.
'Before' and 'after' make the order clear, so past perfect is optional.
Reported speech shifts the tense back: 'He said he was tired'.
connections: Conditionals (v9) use had + participle for unreal past situations.
Prepositions since and for (v2) pair with the perfect tenses.
Reading (v7) depends on noticing which events came first.

check.q: Fill in: 'She ___ (finish) her homework before dinner was ready.'
Which is correct: 'I have seen him last week' or 'I saw him last week'?
check.a: 'I saw him last week': 'last week' is a finished time.

check.q: Fill in: 'I ___ (read) this book twice so far.'
check.a: have read: 'so far' links to now.

cards.title: Articles and prepositions
cards.simple: 'A' and 'an' depend on how the next word sounds, not how it is spelled. 'Hour' starts with the letter h but sounds like 'our', so we say 'an hour'. 'Unit' starts with a vowel letter but sounds like 'yoo-nit', so we say 'a unit'. Prepositions are the little words like in, at and of, and many are glued to a partner: you are good AT maths, not good in maths. In exam words: use an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound, and learn fixed pairs such as good at, fond of, interested in.
cards.idea: Say the next word out loud. 'Hour' sounds like 'our', so it takes **an**: an hour. 'Unit' sounds like 'yoo-nit', so it takes **a**: a unit. The sound decides, not the spelling. Many prepositions are also fixed to a partner word: good at, fond of, interested in.
cards.idea_full:
Say the next word out loud. 'Hour' sounds like 'our', so it takes **an**: an hour. 'Unit' sounds like 'yoo-nit', so it takes **a**: a unit. The sound decides, not the spelling.

The article the is used for something specific or unique (the sun, the best player). Many prepositions are fixed to a partner word: good at, fond of, interested in, afraid of. Since and for are tested often: since goes with a starting point, for goes with a length of time.
cards.definition:
a + consonant sound (a unit, a one-rupee coin). an + vowel sound (an hour, an FM radio).

the: a specific noun, a unique thing, or a superlative (the best).

since + point in time (since 2019). for + length of time (for five years).

Fixed pairs: good at, fond of, interested in, afraid of, angry with (a person), angry at (a thing).

Symbols: 'sound' means the first spoken sound of the next word, not its first letter.
cards.intuition_full: The article a/an exists to keep speech smooth. 'A' before a vowel sound makes an awkward gap, so we slide in an 'n' to link the words: 'an apple'. That is why the first sound matters and not the letter. Words that start with a silent h (hour, honest) begin with a vowel sound. Words that start with a vowel letter but a y or w sound (unit, one) begin with a consonant sound. Prepositions work like glue that has set: native speakers learned the pair together, so there is no rule to derive. A short list of the most common pairs, memorised once, covers most exam questions. For since and for, picture a stopwatch: since names when it started, for names how long it ran.

example.setup: Fill the blanks: '___ hour' and '___ unit'.
steps: Say each word: 'hour' sounds like 'our' and begins with a vowel sound.
So the first blank takes an: an hour.
'Unit' sounds like 'yoo-nit' and begins with a consonant sound.
So the second blank takes a: a unit.

examples.setup: Fill the blanks: '___ hour' and '___ unit'.
steps: Say each word: 'hour' sounds like 'our' and begins with a vowel sound.
So the first blank takes an: an hour.
'Unit' sounds like 'yoo-nit' and begins with a consonant sound.
So the second blank takes a: a unit.

examples.setup: Fill in: 'He is good ___ maths and fond ___ chess.'
steps: 'Good' is followed by at when you talk about a skill: good at.
'Fond' is followed by of: fond of.
Check the other options: good in, fond with and similar pairs are not used.

examples.setup: Fill in: 'She is ___ best player in ___ team.'
steps: 'Best' is a superlative, which needs the: the best.
'Team' here means one specific team already in mind, so the again.
An option like 'a best' fails, because a superlative points to one unique player.

cards.why: Articles and prepositions are quick 1-mark questions, and most are solved by sound or by a memorised pair. In GATE: a sentence with two or three blanks, tested on sound-based a/an, since and for, and fixed pairs.
how: Say the next word aloud and listen for a vowel or consonant sound.
Use the for a specific, unique or superlative noun.
For time, use since with a point and for with a length.
For other prepositions, recall the fixed pair, and test it aloud.
cards.mistake: Choosing a or an from the first letter. 'An university' and 'a hour' look right on paper but sound wrong. Always say the word and choose by the first sound.
edge_cases: 'An honest man' (silent h), 'a European' (y sound).
Letters spoken out: 'an MBA', 'an FM station', 'a UN official'.
No article is needed with plural or uncountable nouns in general statements.
'Angry with' a person but 'angry at' a thing.
connections: Tenses (v1) use since and for with the perfect forms.
Agreement (v3) is the other main grammar check.
Idioms (v6) are fixed word groups in the same way.

check.q: Fill in: '___ one-rupee coin'.
check.a: a: 'one' starts with a w sound.

check.q: Fill in: 'She has lived here ___ ten years.'
check.a: for: ten years is a length.

check.q: Fill in: 'He is afraid ___ dogs.'

cards.title: Agreement and homophones
cards.simple: The verb must match its subject, like a plug fits a socket. In 'The list of items is on the table', the subject is 'list', not 'items', so the verb is 'is'. Words that sound alike but mean different things, like 'their' and 'there', are called homophones. A sentence that sounds right to the ear can still use the wrong one. So check what you mean, not just what you hear. In exam words: subject-verb agreement (singular subject, singular verb), 'neither/nor' agrees with the nearer noun, and homophones are chosen by meaning.
cards.idea: In 'The list of items ___ on the table', the subject is **list**, not items. A single list needs a singular verb: 'is'. Find the real subject, ignoring words in between. Homophones such as their/there/they're sound the same but differ in meaning, so choose by meaning and not by ear.
cards.idea_full:
In 'The list of items ___ on the table', the subject is **list**, not items. A single list needs a singular verb: 'is'. Find the real subject, ignoring phrases in between.

Each, every, either and neither take a singular verb. With 'neither A nor B' or 'either A or B', the verb agrees with the nearer noun. Homophones such as their/there/they're sound the same but differ in meaning, so choose by meaning and not by ear.
cards.definition:
Singular subject + singular verb (the list is). Plural subject + plural verb (the lists are).

Each, every, either, neither + singular verb.

Neither A nor B / either A or B: the verb agrees with B, the nearer noun.

A number of + plural verb. The number of + singular verb.

Homophones: their (belonging to them), there (place), they're (they are); complement (completes), compliment (praise).
cards.intuition_full: The verb is tied to one word, the head of the subject. Phrases that come after it (of items, along with the staff) are decorations. Strip them away and check the remaining word. For 'neither...nor', the sentence says one of two options does not apply, and the speaker looks at the last one named, so the verb follows the closest noun. 'A number of students' means several students, so the verb is plural. 'The number of students' is one number, so the verb is singular. For homophones, the ear is no help since the words sound identical. Read the sentence once for meaning and ask: is this the word for a place, a possession, praise, or a completion?

example.setup: Choose the verb: 'The list of items ___ (is/are) on the table.'
steps: Find the subject by removing the phrase 'of items': 'The list ___ on the table'.
'List' is singular.
A singular subject takes a singular verb: is.

examples.setup: Choose the verb: 'The list of items ___ (is/are) on the table.'
steps: Find the subject by removing the phrase 'of items': 'The list ___ on the table'.
'List' is singular.
A singular subject takes a singular verb: is.

examples.setup: Choose the verb: 'Neither the manager nor the clerks ___ (was/were) late.'
steps: The pair 'neither...nor' is used, so the verb agrees with the nearer noun.
The nearer noun is 'clerks', which is plural.
The verb is the plural form: were.

examples.setup: Choose the verbs: 'A number of students ___ (is/are) absent. The number of students ___ (is/are) forty.'
steps: 'A number of' means several, so the verb is plural: are absent.
'The number of' refers to one number, so the verb is singular: is forty.
The word 'number' is the same in both, but the meaning of the phrase changes the agreement.

cards.why: Agreement errors are easy to hide in a long sentence, and homophones are easy to miss when read quickly. In GATE: choose the correct verb, or spot the wrong sentence among a few.
how: Strip away phrases between the subject and the verb.
Decide whether the real subject is singular or plural.
For each, every, either and neither, use a singular verb.
For sound-alike words, ask what the word means in this sentence.
cards.mistake: Matching the verb to the nearest noun instead of the real subject. In 'The list of items are on the table', 'items' is plural but it is not the subject. Strip the phrase and test the head noun.
edge_cases: 'Neither of the students' takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'neither'.
Collective nouns (committee, team) usually take a singular verb in exam answers: 'The committee has made its decision'.
'Along with' and 'as well as' do not make the subject plural.
Uncountable nouns (information, furniture) are singular.
connections: Tenses (v1) are the other half of verb-form questions.
Vocabulary (v4) overlaps with homophones such as complement/compliment.
Ambiguity (v9) shows how pronouns can mislead in a sentence.

check.q: Choose: 'Each of the players ___ (has/have) a kit.'
Choose: 'Either the teacher or the students ___ (is/are) coming.'
check.a: are, because the nearer noun is students.

check.q: Which is right: 'their' or 'there' in 'Put the books over ___'?

cards.title: Vocabulary
cards.simple: When you meet a hard word, do not panic. The rest of the sentence usually gives hints. In 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it', the second half tells you lucid means easy to understand. Cover the options, guess a meaning from the clues, and then pick the option closest to your guess. Watch out for question words like 'antonym' (the opposite) so that you do not choose the synonym by mistake. In exam words: infer the meaning from context and tone, then match the closest synonym, or the opposite for an antonym question.
cards.idea: Take the sentence 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it.' Everyone understood, so lucid must mean clear. **Context** tells you the meaning even if you have never seen the word. Guess first, then match the closest option. Also check whether the question asks for a synonym or an antonym.
cards.idea_full:
Take the sentence 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it.' Everyone understood, so lucid must mean clear. **Context** tells you the meaning even if you have never seen the word.

Guess a meaning before you look at the options, so the options do not steer you. Check the **tone**: is the word positive or negative? Connectors help: 'despite' and 'but' signal a contrast, and 'because' and 'so' signal a cause. A word may have several meanings, and the sentence picks one.
cards.definition:
Synonym: a word with nearly the same meaning. Antonym: a word with the opposite meaning.

Context clues: a definition clue (a restatement), a contrast clue (but, despite, although), a cause-and-effect clue (so, because), and the tone (positive or negative).

Roots help for unknown words: 'bene-' means good, 'mal-' means bad, 'anti-' means against.
cards.intuition_full: Every sentence is a puzzle with the word as the missing piece. The sentence around it still carries the full meaning, so the gap can usually be filled with a rough synonym. Contrast words are the strongest clues. 'Despite her reticent nature, she spoke at length' tells you reticent is the opposite of 'spoke at length', so it means reserved or quiet. After you have a rough meaning, the options only need to be ranked by closeness. An antonym question flips the target, and the exam places the synonym among the options as a trap. A word like 'cool' or 'sound' has many meanings, so one clue from the sentence decides which one is meant.

example.setup: 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it.' What does 'lucid' mean? (clear / long / loud / angry)
steps: Read the clue: 'so ... that everyone understood it'. The speech was easy to follow.
Guess a meaning before the options: easy to understand.
Match: clear fits. Long, loud and angry say nothing about being understood.

examples.setup: 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it.' What does 'lucid' mean? (clear / long / loud / angry)
steps: Read the clue: 'so ... that everyone understood it'. The speech was easy to follow.
Guess a meaning before the options: easy to understand.
Match: clear fits. Long, loud and angry say nothing about being understood.

examples.setup: 'Despite her reticent nature, she spoke at length at the meeting.' What does 'reticent' mean? (talkative / reserved / angry / proud)
steps: The word 'despite' signals a contrast.
She spoke at length, so reticent describes the opposite quality.
The opposite of 'speaking a lot' is quiet or reserved.
Match: reserved. Talkative is the opposite of the meaning and is the likely decoy.

examples.setup: Find the antonym of 'ephemeral'. (transient / lasting / brief / fleeting)
steps: First get the meaning: ephemeral means lasting a very short time.
Three options (transient, brief, fleeting) are synonyms.
The question asks for the opposite, so choose the option meaning 'long-lasting'.
That is 'lasting'.
examples.answer: lasting. Picking a synonym when the question asks for an antonym is the classic slip.

cards.why: Vocabulary questions reward a calm method over a big word list. In GATE: a synonym, antonym or word-in-context question with four options, where the sentence is the main clue.
how: Read the whole sentence and underline the clue words.
Guess a meaning before reading the options.
Check the tone and any contrast word.
Match the closest option, and recheck whether the question asks for a synonym or antonym.
cards.mistake: Picking a synonym when the question asks for an antonym, or choosing the first familiar-looking word. Read the question word first, and cover the options while you guess.
edge_cases: A word can be positive in one sentence and negative in another.
Two options can be synonyms of each other, so neither is the antonym.
A familiar word can be used in a rare sense (the 'bank' of a river).
Roots and prefixes only suggest the meaning, so confirm with the sentence.
connections: Analogies (v5) use the same synonym, antonym and degree relations.
Idioms (v6) have fixed meanings that context also reveals.
Reading inference (v7) relies on tone and word choice.

check.q: Antonym of 'scarce'?
'The soup was so bland that he added salt.' What does 'bland' mean?
What does 'candid' mean in 'Her candid reply surprised us'?

Guess a meaning before you look at the options, so the options do not steer you. Check the **tone**: is the word positive or negative? Connectors help: 'despite' and 'but' signal a contrast, and 'because' and 'so' signal a cause. A word may have several meanings, and the sentence picks one.

Synonym: a word with nearly the same meaning. Antonym: a word with the opposite meaning.

Context clues: a definition clue (a restatement), a contrast clue (but, despite, although), a cause-and-effect clue (so, because), and the tone (positive or negative).

Roots help for unknown words: 'bene-' means good, 'mal-' means bad, 'anti-' means against.

**Worked example.** 'The speech was so lucid that everyone understood it.' What does 'lucid' mean? (clear / long / loud / angry)

1. Read the clue: 'so ... that everyone understood it'. The speech was easy to follow.
2. Guess a meaning before the options: easy to understand.
3. Match: clear fits. Long, loud and angry say nothing about being understood.

**Answer:** clear.

**Check yourself:** Antonym of 'scarce'?

*Answer:* abundant or plentiful.

cards.title: Analogies
cards.simple: An analogy says 'these two words are related like those two words'. Take whisper and shout. A shout is a very strong whisper, so the link is 'mild to extreme'. Now look at drizzle. Drizzle is mild rain, so we want the extreme version of rain, which is downpour. The trick is to say the link out loud before you look at the options. Be careful not to pick a word that is only about the same topic, like umbrella. In exam words: identify the relation (synonym, antonym, degree, part to whole, tool to user), then pick the option with the same relation in the same direction.
cards.idea: Whisper : Shout :: Drizzle : ?  First say how whisper and shout are linked. A shout is a whisper at the extreme, so the link is **degree**, mild to strong. Drizzle is mild rain, so the answer is the strong form of rain: downpour. Always name the link before you look at the options.
cards.idea_full:
Whisper : Shout :: Drizzle : ?  First say how whisper and shout are linked. A shout is a whisper at the extreme, so the link is **degree**, mild to strong. Drizzle is mild rain, so the answer is the strong form of rain: downpour.

Always name the link before you look at the options. Options on the same subject as the second pair (rain, umbrella) are decoys. Check the direction too: mild to strong is not the same as strong to mild.
cards.definition:
A : B :: C : ? means 'A is to B as C is to ?'.

Common relations: synonym (big : large), antonym (hot : cold), degree (warm : hot), part to whole (petal : flower), tool to its use (knife : cut), worker to workplace (teacher : school), cause to effect (fire : smoke).

The relation must hold in the same direction for both pairs.
cards.intuition_full: An analogy is a template with a hole. The first pair shows the template and the second pair fills it in. Because many words connect in several ways, the exam can build a decoy for each wrong way. 'Whisper : Shout' could be called 'both are sounds', which would let 'Rain' or 'Umbrella' sneak in. Saying the exact link in one short phrase, 'a shout is a very strong whisper', closes that door. Direction is the second guard: 'drizzle to downpour' goes from mild to extreme, and the reverse pair would go downpour to drizzle. Degree analogies have appeared in recent GATE papers, so practise the mild-to-strong and strong-to-mild chains.

steps: Before looking at the options, say how the first pair is linked. Whisper : Shout.
A shout is a whisper turned up to the extreme. The relation is degree: mild to extreme.
Now the second pair. Drizzle is mild rain, so we need the extreme version of the same thing.
Test the options: Rain is just a synonym at medium strength. Umbrella is a tool, a different relation. Downpour fits.
Downpour completes the same relation. Options on the same subject (rain, umbrella) are the usual decoys.

examples.setup: Warm : Hot :: Cool : ? (Mild / Chilly / Cold / Freezing)
steps: Name the link: hot is the stronger form of warm. Degree, one step up.
Cool is where the second pair starts. The answer is the next step up in the cold direction.
Cold is one step up from cool. Freezing is two steps up. Mild and chilly are not stronger.

examples.answer: Cold. One step up in degree, as in the first pair.

examples.setup: Hot : Warm :: Freezing : ? (Cold / Frozen / Chilly / Ice)
steps: Name the link: warm is one step weaker than hot. The direction is down.
Apply to freezing: go one step weaker.
Cold is one step weaker than freezing. Frozen means turned to ice, which is a state, not a weaker degree.
Choose cold.
examples.answer: Cold. The direction reversed (strong to mild), so the pattern from the previous example would not fit.

cards.title: Idioms and phrasal verbs
cards.simple: Some phrases do not mean what their words say. 'Break the ice' has nothing to do with ice. It means to start a friendly conversation with strangers. Phrasal verbs are a verb plus a little word, like give up, and the little word changes the meaning: give up means quit, give in means surrender. You cannot work these out word by word. Read the full sentence, guess what the writer means, and pick the phrase that matches. In exam words: an idiom has a fixed meaning different from its words, and a phrasal verb changes meaning with its particle.
cards.idea: 'Break the ice' has nothing to do with ice. It means to start a friendly conversation. An **idiom** is a fixed phrase whose meaning differs from its words. A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus a small word, and the small word changes the meaning: give up (quit), give in (surrender). Read the whole sentence and choose by meaning.
cards.idea_full:
'Break the ice' has nothing to do with ice. It means to start a friendly conversation. An **idiom** is a fixed phrase whose meaning differs from its words. A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus a small word, and the small word changes the meaning: give up (quit), give in (surrender), give out (distribute).

You cannot work these out word by word. Read the whole sentence, guess what the writer means, then pick the phrase that fits. The same phrasal verb can have different meanings in different sentences.
cards.definition:
Idiom: a fixed group of words with a meaning that is not the sum of its parts (a piece of cake = very easy).

Phrasal verb: verb + particle (up, in, out, off, down), with a meaning that depends on the particle (turn down = reject or reduce).

Meaning is decided by the sentence, so test each option by replacing the phrase with a plain word.
cards.intuition_full: Idioms are word-sized units that happen to be written as several words. Their meaning was fixed by usage over a long time, so no logic on the individual words helps. The reliable method is substitution: replace the phrase with your guess at its meaning and see if the sentence still makes sense. For 'He stayed home as he felt under the weather', replacing with 'slightly ill' keeps the sentence sensible, while 'rainy' does not. Phrasal verbs add a twist, since one verb can pair with many particles and each pair is a different word. 'Turn down' means reject in 'turn down the offer' and reduce in 'turn down the volume'. The sentence tells you which.

example.setup: Meaning of 'gave up' in 'She gave up smoking last year.' (quit / surrendered / handed out / waited)
steps: 'Gave up' is a phrasal verb: give + up.
Substitute each option: 'She quit smoking' makes sense.
'Surrendered smoking' and 'handed out smoking' do not.
So give up here means quit.

examples.setup: Meaning of 'gave up' in 'She gave up smoking last year.' (quit / surrendered / handed out / waited)
steps: 'Gave up' is a phrasal verb: give + up.
Substitute each option: 'She quit smoking' makes sense.
'Surrendered smoking' and 'handed out smoking' do not.
So give up here means quit.

examples.setup: Meaning of 'under the weather' in 'He stayed home as he felt under the weather.' (rainy / slightly ill / angry / lazy)
steps: It is an idiom, so the words alone will not help.
The sentence gives a reason for staying home: he felt something that kept him in.
Substitute: 'felt slightly ill' fits. 'Felt rainy' is meaningless.
So under the weather means a little unwell.

examples.setup: Meaning of 'turn down' in (i) 'She turned down the job offer.' and (ii) 'Please turn down the music.'
steps: In (i) the object is an offer. People accept or reject offers, so turn down means reject.
In (ii) the object is music. You can make music softer, so turn down means reduce the volume.
The same phrasal verb has two meanings, chosen by what follows.

cards.why: Idioms and phrasal verbs are 1-mark meaning questions where guessing from context beats memorising lists. In GATE: pick the meaning of a phrase in a sentence, or fill the blank with the right chunk.
how: Read the whole sentence, not just the phrase.
Guess the meaning from what the sentence is saying.
Replace the phrase with each option and test for sense.
Keep a short list of common phrasal verbs for quick recall.
cards.mistake: Translating the phrase word by word. 'Look into' does not mean looking inside something, it means investigate. Always test by substitution in the full sentence.
edge_cases: The same phrasal verb can have several meanings (turn down, pick up).
Some idioms also have a literal meaning in other sentences.
Particles can be separable: 'turn the offer down'.
British and American idioms sometimes differ.
connections: Vocabulary (v4) uses the same context-clue method.
Sentence order (v8) relies on the same meaning-first approach.
Homophones (v3) are another place where sound can mislead.

cards.title: Reading inference
cards.simple: In an inference question the passage is your only evidence, like a court that allows only the facts shown. Suppose it says prices rose 4% in 2024, slower than in 2023. You can say that prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023. You cannot say prices 'always' rise slowly, because the passage covers only one year. You cannot say what happens in 2025, and you cannot bring in facts about wages. In exam words: choose the option that is directly supported by the text, and strike options with extreme words, predictions beyond the text, or outside facts.
cards.idea: A passage says: 'Prices rose 4% in 2024, slower than in 2023.' Which statement follows? Only what the text says counts. 'Always' is extreme, a claim about 2025 is beyond the text, and wages are an outside fact. The answer is the statement that **restates** the passage: prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023.
cards.idea_full:
A passage says: 'Prices rose 4% in 2024, slower than in 2023.' Which statement follows? Only what the text says counts. 'Always' is extreme, a claim about 2025 is beyond the text, and wages are an outside fact. The answer is the statement that **restates** the passage: prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023.

Treat the passage as the only source of truth. A good inference is a close paraphrase, not a bold guess.
cards.definition:
Valid inference: a statement that must be true if the passage is true.

Traps: extreme words (always, never, all, only), future predictions, outside facts, reversed cause and effect, and the converse of a statement.

A summary covers the main point and nothing the passage does not say.
cards.intuition_full: The passage is a small closed world. Every option is a claim about that world, and your job is to check each claim against the text, like a detective checking an alibi. Extreme words give claims too much reach, since a passage about one year cannot support 'always'. A prediction about the future goes beyond a passage that describes the past. An outside fact may be true in real life but is not in the passage, so it is not an inference. A last subtle trap is the converse: 'All speakers were invited by the committee' does not mean everyone invited spoke. The reliable method is to rephrase the passage in your own words and select the option that says the same thing.

example.setup: Passage: 'Prices rose 4% in 2024, slower than in 2023.' Which follows? (A) Prices always rise slowly. (B) Prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023. (C) Prices will fall in 2025. (D) Wages rose 4% in 2024.
steps: Only what the text says counts, not what seems likely.
'Always' is an extreme word. The passage covers one year, so strike A.
C is about 2025. The text says nothing about the future, so strike C.
D brings in wages, a fact that is not in the passage. Strike D.
B restates the passage: slower than 2023 means a smaller rise in 2024. It is the only option the text supports.

examples.setup: Passage: 'Prices rose 4% in 2024, slower than in 2023.' Which follows? (A) Prices always rise slowly. (B) Prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023. (C) Prices will fall in 2025. (D) Wages rose 4% in 2024.

examples.setup: Passage: 'The library extended its hours to 10 pm after a survey in which 70% of students asked for it.' Which is best supported? (A) All students use the library. (B) The extension followed a student survey. (C) The library will stay open later every year. (D) Most students now study at night.
steps: Restate the passage: a survey was held, 70% asked for longer hours, and the library extended to 10 pm.
A uses 'all': strike. C predicts the future: strike. D is an outside fact about study habits: strike.
B restates the passage: the extension followed a survey.

examples.setup: Passage: 'All the speakers at the event were invited by the committee.' Which must be true? (A) Everyone invited by the committee spoke. (B) Every speaker was invited by the committee. (C) The committee spoke at the event. (D) Some invited people did not attend.
steps: Write the statement as 'speaker implies invited'.
A reverses it: 'invited implies speaker'. This is the converse, not guaranteed.
C and D add new facts. Strike them.
B is the passage itself in other words.
examples.answer: B. A is the converse trap.

cards.why: Inference questions carry 2 marks and are the most frequent verbal pattern. The traps are always the same, so a checklist wins marks. In GATE: a short passage and four statements, one of which is directly supported.
how: Restate the passage in one plain sentence.
Strike options with extreme words (always, never, all, only).
Strike options about the future or outside facts.
Choose the option that is a close paraphrase of the passage.
cards.mistake: Adding outside facts or picking a likely claim the text does not state. Even if an option is true in real life, it is wrong if the passage does not support it. Check each option against a sentence in the text.
edge_cases: 'Most' and 'some' do not imply 'all' or 'none'.
Correlation in the text does not give cause.
A question asking for 'the weakest' or 'not supported' flips the task.
Quotes with figurative words must be translated into plain meaning first.

cards.title: Sentence order and reference
cards.simple: Putting sentences in order is like building a story from jumbled scenes. The first sentence has to make sense on its own. Words like 'he', 'it' and 'this' point back to something already mentioned, so a sentence with them cannot be first. Connectors like 'however' and 'as a result' show how a sentence relates to the one before it. Follow those clues and the order appears. In exam words: choose the opener that needs no earlier sentence, link pronouns to their nouns, and use connectors to chain the rest.
cards.idea: Ravi packed his bag. He drove to the airport. He reached just in time. The sentence with a name and no back-reference comes first. 'He' points back, so it comes later. Find the **opener**, follow the pronouns and connectors, and let the conclusion go last.
cards.idea_full:
Ravi packed his bag. He drove to the airport. He reached just in time. The sentence with a name and no back-reference comes first. 'He' points back, so it comes later.

Find the **opener**, follow the pronouns and connectors, and let the conclusion go last. Connectors such as however, as a result and thus show how a sentence depends on the previous one. Pairs like 'This' plus the thing it refers to usually stay together.
cards.definition:
Opener: a sentence that introduces the topic and has no back-reference (no he, it, this, however at the start).

Reference chain: a pronoun must come after the noun it refers to.

Connectors: however (contrast), as a result and thus (consequence), then and next (sequence), finally (last).

Conclusion: often starts with so, thus or hence.
cards.intuition_full: A paragraph is a chain where each sentence hands something to the next. The first sentence must carry its own context, because there is nothing before it. Pronouns are the easiest tell: a sentence that starts with 'He' or 'This' is a link and cannot be a start. Connectors give direction. 'However' flips the previous idea, 'as a result' follows from it, and 'finally' closes the sequence. When two sentences belong together, for example one mentions an alloy and the next says 'It cracked', glue them and treat the pair as one unit. Then order the units. If two options both look possible, test each order by reading the whole paragraph aloud for flow.

example.setup: Order the sentences: (P) He then drove to the airport. (Q) Ravi packed his bag at dawn. (R) He reached just in time for the flight.
steps: Find the sentence that makes sense alone. Q names Ravi and has no back-reference, so Q is first.
P starts with 'He then', which points back to Ravi and shows the next step.
R says 'He reached', which follows the driving, so R is last.
Order: Q, P, R.

examples.setup: Order the sentences: (P) He then drove to the airport. (Q) Ravi packed his bag at dawn. (R) He reached just in time for the flight.
steps: Find the sentence that makes sense alone. Q names Ravi and has no back-reference, so Q is first.
P starts with 'He then', which points back to Ravi and shows the next step.
R says 'He reached', which follows the driving, so R is last.
Order: Q, P, R.

examples.setup: Order: (1) However, the city's storm drains were blocked. (2) Heavy rain fell on Chennai on Monday. (3) As a result, roads flooded within an hour. (4) Residents were told to stay home.
steps: Sentence 2 introduces the topic with a place and a day, and needs no earlier sentence. It is the opener.
Sentence 1 starts with 'However', a contrast to something already said, so it follows 2.
Sentence 3 starts with 'As a result', a consequence of the drains being blocked, so it follows 1.
Sentence 4 is the final action.

examples.setup: Order: (P) This surprised the lab. (Q) A new alloy was tested on Friday. (R) It cracked under half the expected load. (S) The cause is still unknown.
steps: P starts with 'This', which needs a referent, so P is not first. R starts with 'It', so R is not first. Q is the opener.
R's 'It' refers to the alloy in Q, so R follows Q.
P's 'This' refers to the cracking in R, so P follows R.
S gives the final status, so S is last.
Order: Q, R, P, S.
examples.answer: QRPS. Pronouns chain the sentences: Q to R to P.

cards.why: Ordering questions are rare but quick once you know the method. In GATE: four or five jumbled sentences, tested in 2023 and 2024.
how: Find the sentence that makes sense alone, with no pronoun or connector at the start.
Chain each pronoun to the noun it points to.
Use connectors (however, as a result) to place the next sentence.
Put the conclusion last, and re-read the full order.
cards.mistake: Starting with a sentence that sounds like a conclusion, or one that begins with a pronoun. 'Therefore' and 'This' are links, never openers. Check that every pronoun comes after its noun.
edge_cases: Two sentences with no pronouns may both look like openers; pick the one that sets the scene.
'However' cannot start a paragraph, since it contrasts with an earlier idea.
A sentence with a date can still depend on an earlier event.
Questions with fixed options can be solved by checking only the first sentence.
connections: Reading inference (v7) also needs the argument's flow.
Ambiguity (v9) arises when a pronoun has two possible nouns.
Tenses (v1) help order events in a story.

check.q: Which can be an opener: 'He left early.' or 'Meera left early.'?
check.a: 'Meera left early.' because 'He' needs an earlier mention.

check.q: Where does 'As a result' belong, at the start or after the cause?
Order: (P) She won. (Q) Asha entered the race. (R) She trained for months.

try.label: Try the first sentence ordering question (L2)

cards.what: Ravi packed his bag. He drove to the airport. He reached just in time. The sentence with a name and no back-reference comes first. 'He' points back, so it comes later. Find the **opener**, follow the pronouns and connectors, and let the conclusion go last.
cards.what_full:
Ravi packed his bag. He drove to the airport. He reached just in time. The sentence with a name and no back-reference comes first. 'He' points back, so it comes later.

Find the **opener**, follow the pronouns and connectors, and let the conclusion go last. Connectors such as however, as a result and thus show how a sentence depends on the previous one. Pairs like 'This' plus the thing it refers to usually stay together.

Opener: a sentence that introduces the topic and has no back-reference (no he, it, this, however at the start).

Reference chain: a pronoun must come after the noun it refers to.

Connectors: however (contrast), as a result and thus (consequence), then and next (sequence), finally (last).

Conclusion: often starts with so, thus or hence.

**Worked example.** Order the sentences: (P) He then drove to the airport. (Q) Ravi packed his bag at dawn. (R) He reached just in time for the flight.

1. Find the sentence that makes sense alone. Q names Ravi and has no back-reference, so Q is first.
2. P starts with 'He then', which points back to Ravi and shows the next step.
3. R says 'He reached', which follows the driving, so R is last.
4. Order: Q, P, R.

**Answer:** QPR.

**Check yourself:** Which can be an opener: 'He left early.' or 'Meera left early.'?

*Answer:* 'Meera left early.' because 'He' needs an earlier mention.
cards.trap: Starting with a sentence that sounds like a conclusion, or one that begins with a pronoun. 'Therefore' and 'This' are links, never openers. Check that every pronoun comes after its noun.

cards.title: Conditionals and ambiguity
cards.simple: 'If I were a bird, I would fly to you' is a wish. I am not a bird. Sentences with 'if I were' or 'if I had' describe something that is not real, so you should read the opposite as the truth. Another puzzle is a sentence like 'Mina told Sara that she was late', where 'she' could be either girl. That is called ambiguity. The fix is to name the person instead of using 'she'. In exam words: an unreal conditional implies the opposite fact, and an ambiguous pronoun has more than one possible referent.
cards.idea: 'If I were a bird, I would fly to you.' I am not a bird. A **counterfactual** conditional describes something that is not true, so the real situation is the opposite. A second puzzle is **ambiguity**: in 'Mina told Sara that she was late', the word 'she' could mean either girl.
cards.idea_full:
'If I were a bird, I would fly to you.' I am not a bird. A **counterfactual** conditional describes something that is not true, so the real situation is the opposite. 'If it had rained, we would have stayed' means it did not rain.

A second puzzle is **ambiguity**: in 'Mina told Sara that she was late', the word 'she' could mean either girl. The fix is to repeat the noun. 'Unless' is another logic word: 'unless you study' means 'if you do not study'.
cards.definition:
Open condition (a real possibility): if + present, will + verb. 'If it rains, we stay home.'

Unreal present: if + past (were), would + verb. 'If I were rich, I would travel.' Fact: I am not rich.

Unreal past: if + had + participle, would have + participle. 'If it had rained, we would have stayed.' Fact: it did not rain.

Unless = if not. Ambiguity: a pronoun with two or more possible nouns.
cards.intuition_full: Unreal conditionals are written in a past-looking form on purpose: the grammar signals 'this is not real'. Whenever you see 'if I were' or 'if ... had ...', flip the claim to get the truth. The consequence part is flipped too: 'I would have visited' means I did not visit. 'Unless' compresses a negative condition: 'You will fail unless you study' says if you do not study, you fail. Ambiguity is a different issue. A pronoun is a stand-in for the last suitable noun, and when two nouns fit, the reader cannot decide. A sentence is clear only if exactly one noun can fit. The usual cure is to replace the pronoun with the noun, or to restructure the sentence.

example.setup: 'If I were a bird, I would fly to you.' What can you infer? (I am a bird / I am not a bird / I can fly / You are a bird)
steps: The condition uses 'if I were', which is an unreal present.
An unreal condition describes something that is not true.
So the fact is the opposite: I am not a bird.

examples.setup: 'If I were a bird, I would fly to you.' What can you infer? (I am a bird / I am not a bird / I can fly / You are a bird)
steps: The condition uses 'if I were', which is an unreal present.
An unreal condition describes something that is not true.
So the fact is the opposite: I am not a bird.

examples.setup: 'You will fail unless you study.' Which means the same? (If you study you will fail / If you do not study you will fail / If you fail you will study / You will study and fail)
steps: 'Unless' means 'if not'.
Replace it: 'You will fail if you do not study.'
Check the others: the first reverses the meaning, the third swaps cause and result.
examples.answer: If you do not study you will fail.

examples.setup: 'Mina told Sara that she was late.' Is it ambiguous? Rewrite it clearly.
steps: The pronoun 'she' can refer to Mina or to Sara.
Two nouns fit, so the reader cannot tell who was late.
Repeat the noun: 'Mina told Sara that Sara was late.'
examples.answer: Yes, it is ambiguous. Naming the person removes the ambiguity.

cards.why: Conditionals and ambiguity test careful reading of exactly what is said. In GATE: an unreal conditional with an inference, or a sentence where a pronoun is unclear.
how: Spot 'if I were' or 'if ... had ...': it is unreal.
Flip the claim to get the real fact.
For 'unless', replace it with 'if not'.
For pronouns, list the nouns that fit. More than one means ambiguous.
cards.mistake: Reading a counterfactual as true. 'If I had known, I would have visited' means I did not know and did not visit. Always flip the claim.
edge_cases: 'If I were' uses were even for 'I'.
'Unless' is not the same as 'if', since it negates the condition.
A pronoun is ambiguous only if two nouns are possible.
'Only if' is a one-way condition.
connections: Tenses (v1) supply the had + participle form.
Conditional logic (ga.analytical n8) formalises these statements.
Reading inference (v7) uses the same flip when a counterfactual is the premise.

check.q: 'If she had called, I would have answered.' Did she call?
Rewrite with if: 'You cannot enter unless you have a pass.'
check.a: You cannot enter if you do not have a pass.

check.q: 'Ravi told Amit that he had won.' Ambiguous?
check.a: Yes, 'he' can be Ravi or Amit.

Asked: 2021 CS1 Q3

scenes.title: Past perfect marks the earlier past event

objects.text:
The train ___ (leave)
before we reached the station.

steps.caption: Two things happened in the past. Put them on a time line and ask which came first.
'We reached the station' is the later event. It uses the simple past: reached.
The train left earlier than that. It is a past event that happened before another past event.
The earlier past takes the past perfect: had + past participle. So the blank is 'had left'.

scenes.title: Analogy: name the relation, then apply it

steps.caption: Whisper : Shout. Before looking at options, say how the first pair is linked.
Both are speaking, but a shout is a whisper turned up to the extreme. The relation is degree: mild to extreme.
Now the second pair. Drizzle is mild rain, so we need the extreme version of the same thing.
Test each option against 'mild to extreme': Rain is just a synonym at medium strength. Umbrella is a tool, a different relation. Downpour fits.
Downpour completes the same relation. Options on the same subject (rain, umbrella) are the usual decoys.

objects.text:
Prices rose 4% in 2024,
slower than in 2023.

objects.label: Prices rose less in 2024 than in 2023

steps.caption: Which statement follows from the passage? Only what the text says counts, not what seems likely.
'Always' is an extreme word. The passage covers one year, so it cannot support 'always'. Strike A.
C is about 2025. The text says nothing about the future, so C goes beyond the passage. Strike it.
D brings in wages, a fact that is not in the passage. Using outside facts is the other common trap. Strike D.
B restates the passage: slower than 2023 means a smaller rise in 2024. It is the only option the text supports.

scenes.title: An or a? Listen to the first sound

objects.text: vowel sound -> an   |   consonant sound -> a

steps.caption: Say each word: 'hour' sounds like 'our' and begins with a vowel sound.
So the first blank takes an: an hour.
'Unit' sounds like 'yoo-nit' and begins with a consonant sound.
So the second blank takes a: a unit.  **Answer:** an hour, a unit.

scenes.title: Find the subject, then match the verb

steps.caption: Find the subject by removing the phrase 'of items': 'The list ___ on the table'.
'List' is singular.
A singular subject takes a singular verb: is.  **Answer:** is.

scenes.title: Use the context clue to define the word

steps.caption: Read the clue: 'so ... that everyone understood it'. The speech was easy to follow.
Guess a meaning before the options: easy to understand.
Match: clear fits. Long, loud and angry say nothing about being understood.  **Answer:** clear.

scenes.title: Phrasal verb: test each meaning in the sentence

steps.caption: 'Gave up' is a phrasal verb: give + up.
Substitute each option: 'She quit smoking' makes sense.
'Surrendered smoking' and 'handed out smoking' do not.

set.text:
'surrendered smoking' and
'handed out smoking' make no sense

steps.caption: So give up here means quit.  **Answer:** quit.

scenes.title: Order the sentences: who is named, what follows

objects.label: P: He then drove to the airport.
Q: Ravi packed his bag at dawn.
R: He reached just in time for the flight.

steps.caption: Find the sentence that makes sense alone. Q names Ravi and has no back-reference, so Q is first.

set.text:
Q names Ravi and points back to nothing:
it comes first

steps.caption: P starts with 'He then', which points back to Ravi and shows the next step.

set.text:
P: 'He then' points back to Ravi
and gives the next step

steps.caption: R says 'He reached', which follows the driving, so R is last.

set.text:
R: 'He reached' follows the driving:
it comes last

steps.caption: Order: Q, P, R.  **Answer:** QPR.
